newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. plans emergency airlift for fleeing Afghans.
newsitem.headline: U.N. plans emergency airlift for fleeing Afghans.

text.p: A U.N. refugee agency said on Tuesday it hoped to airlift supplies to thousands of Afghans displaced by fighting in northwest Afghanistan.
"The harsh winter weather has added a new element of urgency to the situation," said Rupert Colville, an Islamabad-based spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
He said 700 to 800 Afghans were arriving daily from the embattled province of Badghis in the western city of Herat, where three hastily built camps already housed 8,300 people.
By Monday night, 1,500 people had moved into one camp that had opened the day before. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of other people may have found shelter with relatives, Colville said.

"There was a heavy snowfall in (the Badghis provincial capital) Qala-i-Nau yesterday," he said. "The fear is that with night temperatures close to zero in lowland areas and snow in higher areas, health risks will increase dramatically for people living in the open or travelling across rough country."

He said the UNHCR had asked the Taleban militia, which controls Herat, to provide transport planes for the proposed airlift. "The initial response has been positive," he said, but could not say when the operation might start.
The UNHCR estimates that up to 50,000 Afghans may have fled their homes in Badghis to escape recent fighting between the Taleban and the forces of northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The radical Islamic militia is trying to push east through Badghis into Dostum's northern heartland. A Taleban defeat could make Herat vulnerable to an attack by Dostum and his allies.
U.N. sources say both sides have used planes, tanks and heavy artillery in see-saw battles that have raged along the Murghab river and elsewhere for more than two weeks.

Colville said the airlift would take tents and other urgently needed relief items to Herat. U.N. agencies there had enough food stocks for the moment, but the UNHCR could run out of tents within five days if displaced people kept coming.

He said the Taleban authorities in Herat had agreed to release 50 tonnes of wheat which the UNHCR would pay to have transported along a potholed road to the remote town of Qala-i-Nau, about 130 km (81 miles) to the northeast.
Supplies from a convoy that reached Qala-i-Nau 10 days ago were still being distributed to displaced people in the area.
Trucks carrying 7,850 blankets were expected to arrive in Herat later on Tuesday after a gruelling 10-day trip across Afghanistan, Colville said.
